title: Nasopharyngeal carriage and antibiotic susceptibility patterns of streptococcus pneumoniae, haemophilus influenzae, moraxella catarrhalis and staphylococcus aureus among urban Ugandan children post-PCV10 introduction: a cross-sectional study.
ehr_evidence: Nasopharyngeal samples were collected from the children by using single sterile swabs... sent to the Clinical Microbiology Laboratory at Makerere University College of Health Sciences; an interviewer-assisted questionnaire was used to collect clinical and demographic data, entered into Epidata and exported to SPSS v17.0.
summary: A cross-sectional study of 194 urban Ugandan children aged 6-60 months at Mulago Assessment Centre clinic in Kampala, 5 years post-PCV10 introduction, assessing nasopharyngeal carriage and antibiotic susceptibility of S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, and S. aureus.
key_findings: Overall carriage prevalence was 62% (120/194), significantly associated with a history of antibiotic use (chi-square=5.95, p=0.0159) and respiratory symptoms (chi-square=12.79, p=0.0003).
Species carriage prevalence was 46% (90/194) for S. pneumoniae, 21% (40/194) for H. influenzae, 7% (14/194) for M. catarrhalis, and 6% (12/194) for S. aureus.
Species co-carriage occurred in 17% (32/194), predominantly multidrug-resistant S. pneumoniae + H. influenzae (23 children); S. pneumoniae + S. aureus co-carriage was not detected.
Pneumococci were highly resistant to cotrimoxazole (100%), erythromycin (76%), and tetracycline (52%), with 42% (81/194) multidrug-resistant.
MRSA was not detected; S. aureus was resistant to penicillin (100%) and co-trimoxazole.
Post-PCV10, there was a decrease in S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis, and S. aureus carriage and an increase in H. influenzae carriage, alongside increased antimicrobial resistance.
captured_features: Household crowding (number of persons in household)
population: Children aged 6-60 months attending the children's outpatient clinic at Mulago Hospital Assessment Centre, Kampala, Uganda
exposure_domain: Vaccination (PCV10), antibiotic exposure, respiratory infections, and household/social factors (crowding, smoking)
limitations: 52 isolates were not recovered, leaving a small sample size of 194 children.
Pneumococci were not serotyped, so VT serotype coverage could not be assessed.
No clinical evaluation was performed to determine whether the isolated bacteria were clinically relevant.
Comparison with prior Ugandan studies is limited because those studied healthy children while this study used sick children.
